name: Chewing and spitting
lead: Chewing and spitting (CHSP) is a behaviour in which a person chews food for its taste and then spits it out without swallowing. In the clinical literature it is described as a compensatory or purging-type behaviour in people with eating disorders, and the reason people report doing it is weight control: it lets them taste food while limiting what they take in, in pursuit of a thinner body. In that sense it is a weight-and-appearance behaviour, and the research describes it as a feature of eating disorders rather than as a technique.

In a 1985 study of 275 patients meeting criteria for bulimia, 64.5 percent reported chewing and spitting out food, alongside binge eating (100 percent), self-induced vomiting (88.1 percent), laxative use (60.6 percent) and diuretic use (33.1 percent) [1]. A 2002 comparison found it in 22 percent of eating-disorder patients [3], and a 2015 study of 359 patients found 24.5 percent had used it as a compensatory behaviour to lose weight [5].

A 2016 systematic review identified nine studies, all of clinical samples and most of low quality, and found no studies of treatment [8]. Studies report it as an indicator of overall eating-disorder severity [6][8]. Support for eating-disorder concerns is available through clinicians and eating-disorder services.

paras: Chewing and spitting involves putting food in the mouth, chewing it and expelling it rather than swallowing. Clinical papers treat it as a compensatory behaviour alongside vomiting, laxative use and excessive exercise, and some describe it as a neglected symptom that appears in few diagnostic criteria [7]. A 1997 case report described a 19-year-old woman whose main symptom was chewing and spitting, which she chose as the best strategy to avoid weight gain while enjoying the taste of large quantities of food [4].

In the 1985 study of 275 patients with bulimia, mean age was 24.8 years and average illness duration about seven years, and 64.5 percent reported chewing and spitting [1]. A 2002 study that compared patients who reported it with those who did not found it in 22 percent of eating-disorder patients, with more severe eating-related pathology in anorexia nervosa and in eating disorder not otherwise specified; in bulimia nervosa patients, it was associated only with greater distortion of body image, and binging was not related to it in any diagnostic group [3].

A study of 324 inpatients on a behavioural eating-disorder unit found a third (107) reported it in the eight weeks before admission and 21 percent (69) at least weekly. The weekly group engaged in more restricting, diet pill and laxative use and excessive exercise, and reported greater drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction, depression and neuroticism; 70 percent of them reported loss of control [6]. A study of 359 patients found 24.5 percent had used it as a compensatory behaviour, and that group showed more severe symptoms and suicidal behaviours alongside higher drive for thinness, craving and impulse-regulation scores [5].

Peer-reviewed papers have studied the behaviour as a clinical feature of bulimia (1988), among eating-disordered patients (2002), in relation to binge eating (2004), as a compensatory behaviour (2015) and as a marker of psychopathology and behavioural severity in inpatients (2015) [2][3][9][5][6]. The 2016 systematic review reported that it appears more often in restrictive-type disorders such as anorexia nervosa than in binge-type disorders, and more often in younger people [8]. It has also been examined in eating behaviour 18 to 35 months after gastric bypass surgery [10], and a 1989 report linked it to a protein-sparing modified fast and psychosocial stressors [11].

Human clinical studies exist, but they are observational descriptions of patients with eating disorders; none tests it as an appearance technique, and the 2016 systematic review found no studies of treatment [8]. The 1985 study of 275 patients with bulimia reported its frequency [1], and cross-sectional studies of 324 inpatients and 359 patients examined its associations with severity [5][6].

card.summary: An eating-disorder behaviour studied in clinics as a marker of severity, not a researched appearance method.
card.note: Described in the literature as a compensatory behaviour associated with eating disorders; support is available through clinicians.

quick.overview:
Chewing and spitting means chewing food and spitting it out instead of swallowing. In research it is documented as a behaviour in people with eating disorders, such as bulimia.

Published studies are clinical descriptions of patients; none tests it as a way to improve appearance.
quick.mechanism: Studies describe it as a compensatory behaviour used to avoid calorie intake while experiencing taste, and it has been linked to binge eating.
quick.risks: Papers report it as a marker of greater psychopathology and behavioural severity in inpatients with eating disorders [6]. Anyone affected can seek help from a clinician or an eating-disorder helpline.

angle.goal: Weight and body shape (as reported by patients)

angle.text: Case reports describe patients choosing chewing and spitting as a strategy to avoid gaining weight while enjoying the taste of large amounts of food [4]. The literature documents it as a symptom of eating disorders associated with greater severity, and the wiki records it as a documented behaviour rather than a method.
